blocks.text: Scenario A — History taking
A 27-year-old woman presents with progressively worsening dysmenorrhoea and pelvic pain. Take a focused history and discuss the likely diagnosis.
Scenario B — Suspected deep endometriosis
A 32-year-old woman reports painful defaecation during menstruation, deep dyspareunia and chronic pelvic pain. Outline your investigations and management.
Scenario C — Endometrioma
A 29-year-old woman has an ovarian cyst with ultrasound features suggestive of an endometrioma. Explain the findings and discuss treatment options.
Scenario D — Infertility counselling
A 31-year-old woman with known endometriosis has been trying to conceive for two years. Discuss fertility assessment and treatment options.
Endometriosis is an oestrogen-dependent inflammatory disease. Its exact origin is not fully established, and multiple biological mechanisms may contribute.
Common anatomical patterns include:
1. Superficial peritoneal endometriosis
Lesions occur on the pelvic peritoneum and may cause pain despite being small or difficult to see on imaging.
2. Ovarian endometrioma
An endometriosis-associated ovarian cyst containing old blood, often called a chocolate cyst.
3. Deep endometriosis
Disease extending into tissues beneath the peritoneal surface. It can involve the uterosacral ligaments, rectovaginal region, bowel or urinary tract.
The extent of visible disease does not reliably predict pain severity. A patient with limited lesions can experience debilitating symptoms, while extensive disease may cause relatively few symptoms.
Start with a professional introduction.

“Good morning. My name is …, and I am a medical doctor. I understand that you have been experiencing pelvic pain. I would like to ask about the pattern of your pain, your periods, bowel and urinary symptoms, and whether it has affected your daily activities or fertility. Some questions may be personal, but they will help us identify the possible cause and discuss suitable treatment. Is that okay?”

blocks.text: If the patient has sudden severe pain, collapse, fever or possible pregnancy with pain, prioritise urgent assessment rather than proceeding through a routine chronic-pain history.

Rectal bleeding also requires assessment for gastrointestinal conditions rather than being automatically attributed to endometriosis.

blocks.text: Endometriosis can affect fertility through inflammation, adhesions, distortion of pelvic anatomy and, in some cases, reduced ovarian reserve.

blocks.text: A tender abdominal wall nodule near a caesarean-section scar can suggest abdominal wall endometriosis, although other diagnoses must be considered.
With consent, privacy and a chaperone, perform an examination when clinically indicated.
Speculum examination may identify vaginal or cervical lesions, bleeding or another explanation for symptoms.

blocks.text: A normal examination does not rule out endometriosis.
Example 1 — Suspected uncomplicated endometriosis

“The patient is haemodynamically stable. Abdominal examination reveals mild lower abdominal tenderness without guarding or a palpable mass. Pelvic examination, if performed and tolerated, does not reveal a definite structural abnormality. Given the history of progressive dysmenorrhoea and deep dyspareunia, endometriosis remains a significant clinical possibility despite the absence of specific examination findings.”
Example 2 — Suspected deep endometriosis

“Pelvic examination reveals posterior pelvic tenderness, reduced uterine mobility and nodularity along the uterosacral ligament region. In the context of cyclical dyschezia and deep dyspareunia, these findings raise suspicion of deep endometriosis. I would arrange specialist imaging and referral to an appropriate gynaecology service.”
Example 3 — Suspected endometrioma

“An adnexal mass is palpable on examination. Given the history of dysmenorrhoea and chronic pelvic pain, an endometrioma is a differential diagnosis. Pelvic ultrasound is required to characterise the mass and guide further management.”

blocks.text: Do not overlook an acute emergency in a patient already known to have endometriosis. New pain may have a different cause.
The aim is to support the diagnosis, assess the location and extent of disease, identify complications and guide treatment.
First-line imaging in many patients

Transvaginal ultrasound is generally preferred when appropriate and acceptable. It can identify ovarian endometriomas, some deep endometriosis and alternative pelvic pathology. Transabdominal ultrasound is an alternative or complement.

Reduced ovarian mobility or other signs of adhesions.

blocks.text: The appearance of an ovarian mass must be interpreted by an appropriately trained clinician; not every complex ovarian cyst is an endometrioma.
Useful for selected cases
MRI can help map deep endometriosis, assess complex anatomy and plan surgery. It is not routinely necessary for every patient with suspected endometriosis.

content_groups.group_title: D. Does the patient need laparoscopy to confirm endometriosis?

blocks.text: Not necessarily.
Endometriosis can be diagnosed and treated through a clinical pathway without immediate surgery. Consider laparoscopy when:

items.text: Symptoms persist despite appropriate empirical treatment.
Hormonal treatment is unsuitable or unacceptable.
Imaging is negative but clinical suspicion remains.
Surgical diagnosis or treatment is being considered.
Fertility or complex disease considerations make surgery appropriate.

blocks.text: Histology may support the diagnosis when lesions are biopsied, but a negative biopsy does not invariably exclude disease.
Important: A normal ultrasound or MRI does not exclude superficial peritoneal endometriosis.
Treatment depends on the severity of symptoms, disease location, previous response to treatment, contraindications and whether the patient wishes to conceive.

items.text: Assess for urgent complications and alternative diagnoses.
Discuss pain control and the impact on daily life.
Offer analgesia when appropriate.
Discuss hormonal treatment if pregnancy is not currently desired and there are no contraindications.
Arrange imaging and specialist referral when indicated.
Agree on follow-up to assess treatment response.

blocks.text: NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen or naproxen, may be used for pain when suitable.
Consider contraindications, including relevant renal disease, peptic ulcer disease, bleeding disorders and allergy.

Paracetamol may be an alternative or adjunct in selected patients. Persistent pain despite appropriate analgesia should prompt reassessment rather than indefinite escalation without investigating the cause.
Hormonal treatments aim to reduce endometriosis-associated pain, often by suppressing menstruation or ovarian hormonal stimulation.
1. Combined hormonal contraception
Combined oral contraceptive pills, including continuous regimens in suitable patients, may reduce dysmenorrhoea and other pain symptoms. Check eligibility and contraindications.
2. Progestogens
Oral progestogens, progestogen-only contraception and the LNG-IUS are options for selected patients. They may reduce pain and menstrual bleeding.
3. GnRH agonists or antagonists

These may be considered for persistent symptoms when first-line options are ineffective or unsuitable. Specialist supervision is required because of hypo-oestrogenic effects and potential bone loss; add-back therapy may be needed.
Hormonal treatment can improve pain but does not eradicate all lesions, and symptoms may recur after treatment is stopped.
Hormonal suppression should not be prescribed as a fertility treatment for a patient actively trying to conceive, because it prevents or suppresses ovulation during use.
Surgery may be considered for persistent symptoms, endometriomas, deep disease, organ involvement or selected fertility-related indications.

items.text: Laparoscopic excision or ablation of visible endometriosis.
Excision of an ovarian endometrioma in selected patients.
Adhesiolysis when appropriate.
Specialist surgery for deep endometriosis involving bowel, bladder or ureters.
Hysterectomy in selected patients who have completed their family and have persistent symptoms despite appropriate treatment.

blocks.text: Surgery should be individualised. Deep endometriosis may require a multidisciplinary team involving gynaecologists with specialist expertise and, where necessary, colorectal or urological surgeons.

content_groups.group_title: E. Important counselling about endometrioma surgery

blocks.text: Excision of an ovarian endometrioma can reduce ovarian reserve, particularly when cysts are bilateral or surgery is repeated.

items.text: Current fertility plans.
Ovarian reserve and the potential impact of surgery.
Whether conservative management is reasonable.
Recurrence risk.
The possibility of fertility preservation in selected patients.

blocks.text: Surgery should not be performed solely because an endometrioma is present without considering its characteristics, symptoms, fertility goals and the risks of intervention.
Endometriosis does not mean a patient cannot conceive. Management should consider age, ovarian reserve, tubal anatomy, semen analysis, duration of infertility and the patient's preferences.

items.text: Assess both partners. Obtain an appropriate fertility history and arrange semen analysis.
Assess tubal patency when indicated, using hysterosalpingography or another suitable test.
Evaluate ovarian reserve selectively. AMH and antral follicle count may assist treatment planning but do not reliably predict spontaneous conception on their own.
Discuss expectant management when appropriate, considering age, symptoms and duration of infertility.
Consider surgery selectively. Operative treatment may improve the chance of spontaneous pregnancy in some patients, but ovarian surgery can reduce ovarian reserve.
Consider assisted reproduction. IVF may be appropriate depending on age, tubal disease, ovarian reserve, semen findings and previous treatment.

blocks.text: Hormonal suppression alone does not improve fertility while a patient is actively trying to conceive.

items.text: Chronic pelvic pain and impaired quality of life.
Subfertility or infertility.
Ovarian endometriomas.
Pelvic adhesions and distorted anatomy.
Deep bowel or urinary tract involvement.
Ureteric obstruction and potential renal damage in severe urinary tract disease.
Psychological distress, anxiety and depression.
Recurrence of symptoms after treatment.

blocks.text: Endometriosis is associated with an increased relative risk of certain ovarian cancers, but the absolute risk remains low. It is not an indication for routine ovarian cancer screening in every patient.

subsections.subsection_title: 11. Counselling a patient with suspected endometriosis

blocks.text: “Your symptoms suggest that you may have endometriosis. This is a condition in which tissue similar to the lining of the womb grows elsewhere in the pelvis, potentially causing inflammation, pain and sometimes fertility difficulties.

We can usually begin by assessing your symptoms and arranging an ultrasound scan. If the scan is normal, endometriosis may still be present, so further assessment may be appropriate if your symptoms continue.

Treatment options include painkillers, hormonal medication and surgery in selected cases. The right option depends on how much the condition affects your life, the location of any disease and whether you wish to become pregnant.
If you are planning pregnancy, we will take particular care to balance fertility treatment against the potential effects of surgery on your ovarian reserve.
I would also like to discuss how the pain affects your daily life and agree on a plan for follow-up.”
A condition in which tissue similar to the endometrium occurs outside the uterus, producing an inflammatory response that may cause pain, adhesions and infertility.

content_groups.group_title: Question 2: What are the classic symptoms?

blocks.text: Dysmenorrhoea, chronic pelvic pain, deep dyspareunia, cyclical dyschezia and subfertility.

content_groups.group_title: Question 3: Does a normal ultrasound exclude endometriosis?

blocks.text: No. Superficial peritoneal disease may not be visible on ultrasound or MRI.
No. CA-125 may be elevated in endometriosis but lacks sufficient specificity for diagnosis and should not be used to diagnose the condition.

content_groups.group_title: Question 5: What is first-line treatment for pain?

blocks.text: An NSAID and/or hormonal treatment, depending on contraindications, symptoms and fertility plans.

content_groups.group_title: Question 6: When should deep endometriosis be referred to a specialist centre?

blocks.text: When bowel, bladder or ureteric involvement is suspected, or when complex disease requires specialist imaging and multidisciplinary surgical planning.

content_groups.group_title: Question 7: Why can endometrioma surgery affect fertility?

blocks.text: Surgery can remove or damage healthy ovarian tissue and reduce ovarian reserve, particularly with bilateral or repeat procedures.

content_groups.group_title: Question 8: Does hormonal suppression improve fertility while a patient is trying to conceive?

blocks.text: No. Hormonal suppression treats pain but does not improve spontaneous conception while it is being used to suppress reproductive function.
